opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a real tension, and I'd rather face it honestly than pretend it doesn't exist.

The models are getting more general very quickly. Each new generation absorbs things that used to need a separate product: retrieval, coding help, document analysis, even parts of agent workflows. So if your tool is just a thin layer of prompt engineering or a nicer interface on top of a model, you're in a fragile position. The next model release, or the model company's own app, can erase that gap almost overnight. We've already seen this happen many times.

But I don't think that means there's no room for tools. It means the source of value has to shift. A few things seem durable to me.

First, **context and environment**. A general model is only as useful as what it can see and act on. Tools that connect deeply to a specific environment, like a company's codebase, its data systems, or the real workflows people use every day, are building something the model alone doesn't have. As models get stronger, this layer actually becomes more valuable, because a capable model with the right context and the right actions can do far more.

Second, **feedback loops**. If a tool is where real tasks happen and real outcomes get measured, it produces signals about what success looks like in that domain. That's very hard to replicate from outside. In some sense, the tools that own the evaluation and the iteration loop own a piece of the intelligence too.

Third, **taking responsibility for the outcome, not just the interaction**. Model companies mostly sell capability. Many users don't want capability. They want a result they can trust. Owning reliability, verification, and accountability in a vertical is real work, and generality doesn't automatically solve it.

From the model side, our view is that the model itself increasingly *is* the product. So we try hard to push capability, especially long context, reasoning, and agentic ability, as far as we can. But the ecosystem shouldn't be zero-sum. A stronger base model expands the space of what tools can do. The question for any builder is simple: when the next model comes out, does your product get better or does it get replaced? If it gets better, you're probably building in the right place.

r001.rationale: The response says, “I don’t think that means there’s no room for tools,” and describes durable sources of value for them.

r002.rationale: It says each new model absorbs capabilities once needing a separate product, and warns that a model company’s own app can erase the advantage of a thin tool layer.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the space for tools keeps moving, and you have to be clear-eyed about which direction it moves.

When a model becomes more general, a lot of things that used to be "a product" collapse into "a feature of the model." Two years ago you could build a company around summarization, or around a chat interface with a bit of prompt engineering on top. Today the base model does that natively, and the first-party product from the lab does it with better distribution and a better feedback loop than you'll ever have. So if your tool is essentially a thin wrapper that adds a little structure around a capability the model already has, you are betting against the lab's roadmap, and the lab's roadmap is usually faster than yours. I don't think that's a good bet.

But that doesn't mean there's no room. It means the room shifts. There are a few places where I think it's still very real.

One is where the value depends on context the lab doesn't have and can't easily get. A model is general; your users' data, workflows, permissions, and history are not. If you sit on a real workflow, you know the state of the world in a way a general assistant doesn't, and you can turn that into something the model alone can't produce. That's not a wrapper, that's actually doing the integration work the lab has no incentive to do for a vertical.

The second is where the problem is long-horizon and agentic. The models are getting good at reasoning over many steps, but turning that into something reliable in a real environment is still a lot of engineering: tool interfaces, verification, recovery when something goes wrong, the harness around the model. The first-party products are solving this for the broadest cases. The long tail of environments, each with its own tooling and constraints, is enormous, and I don't think any one company covers it.

The third is just distribution and trust. In some domains, who you are matters more than what the model can do. Enterprise, regulated industries, places where people need to know where their data goes. The first-party product may be technically excellent and still not be the thing those customers adopt.

So my framing would be: don't build on the assumption that the model stays where it is. Build assuming it gets significantly better, and ask whether your product becomes more valuable or less valuable when that happens. If a stronger model makes you obsolete, you're in the wrong place. If a stronger model makes your product better, because you've built the context and the workflow and the trust that lets that capability actually land somewhere, then you're in a good position, and honestly the labs shipping better models is the best thing that can happen to you.

And from our own side, as a company that builds models, I'd say we actually want that ecosystem to exist. The model being general doesn't mean we know how to apply it everywhere. The people building tools are the ones who find out what the model is actually good for, and that feedback comes back into the model. So I don't see it as purely competitive. It's more that the line keeps moving, and you have to keep asking which side of it you're on.

r001.rationale: The response says there is still room to build tools, while explaining that the opportunity shifts as models become more general.

r002.rationale: It says that as models become more general, products built around existing capabilities can collapse into model features, and first-party products can offer those capabilities with stronger distribution.

astra-6.text:
I think the opportunity is still very large, but you have to be careful about what you’re building around. If your product mainly compensates for something the model cannot do today, then a better model might make that product unnecessary. The more interesting question is: as models become more capable, does your product become more valuable?

For example, being able to generate a good answer is different from completing a task inside a company. You need the right context, access to systems, and some way to check whether the work was done correctly. There’s room to build around that whole process. But simply connecting a model to a few tools probably isn’t a durable advantage by itself.

First-party products will keep expanding, so I wouldn’t assume there’s a fixed boundary they won’t cross. I would start with a specific user and a problem you understand deeply. Can you deliver a substantially better outcome, and can you keep improving through actual usage? Ideally, each improvement in the underlying model lets you solve more of that user’s problem. Then model progress is helping your business grow.

r001.rationale: The response says the opportunity to build is “still very large” as models become more capable.

r002.rationale: It says first-party products will keep expanding and may make products based on model limitations unnecessary, but does not state that more general-purpose third-party tools are likely to overlap more with first-party products.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: as the model gets better, does your product become more useful, or does the reason for your product disappear? If you’re mainly compensating for something the model cannot do today, that can be a difficult position, because the next model may solve it directly.

But more general intelligence also makes it possible to build tools that weren’t practical before. You can go deeper into a workflow, connect to the right data, and help users complete a task from beginning to end. The model provides a capability; turning that capability into something reliable and useful still requires a lot of work.

So I wouldn’t view it simply as competing with the model companies. I would look for a user need where better models strengthen the product, and where you can keep learning from actual usage. Of course, the boundary will keep moving. You have to build with that in mind.

r001.rationale: It says more general intelligence makes tools possible that were not practical before and advises finding needs where better models strengthen the product.

r002.rationale: It mentions competing with model companies and a moving boundary, but does not state that third-party tools become more likely to overlap with first-party products as they become more general-purpose.
